title: Rebirth Treatise (Upadeśa on the Sūtra of Immeasurable Life, with the Verses of Aspiration for Birth)
title_original: 無量壽經優波提舍願生偈
alt_titles: Wuliangshou jing lun 無量壽經論 (colophon)

attribution.tradition: Composed by the bodhisattva Vasubandhu (Posoupandou 婆藪槃豆, Tianqin 天親) and translated by Bodhiruci in the Northern Wei
attribution.scholarly: Extant only in Chinese; whether its author is the Yogācāra Vasubandhu is debated

structure.description: 24 five-character quatrains (96 lines) of aspiration, then prose: the five gates of mindfulness, the 29 adornments (17 of the land, 8 of the Buddha, 4 of the bodhisattvas), the one dharma-phrase, skilful transfer, the five gates of merit (T26 230c–233a)

summary: Vasubandhu's verses of aspiration to be born in Sukhāvatī ('World-honoured One, with single mind I take refuge in the Tathāgata of Unhindered Light filling the ten directions and aspire to be born in the Land of Peace and Bliss') and their explanation: whoever perfects the five gates of mindfulness — worship, praise (calling the name), aspiration (śamatha), contemplation (vipaśyanā) of the 29 adornments, and transfer of merit — will be born there and see Amitābha; the adornments enter the one pure phrase, the uncreated dharma-body of true wisdom; the five practices bring five gates of merit, the last being the return to the forest of passions to teach beings.

title: Commentary on the Rebirth Treatise (Wangsheng lun zhu)
title_original: 無量壽經優婆提舍願生偈註
alt_titles: Wangsheng lun zhu 往生論註
Jingtu lun zhu 淨土論註

structure.description: 2 fascicles; fasc. 1 on the verses, fasc. 2 on the prose; ends with the 'three vows' (11th, 18th, 22nd) proving other-power

summary: Tanluan's commentary opens with Nāgārjuna's difficult and easy paths — the easy path being to aspire to birth through faith in the Buddha and to be carried by the power of his vow into the rightly established group of the Mahāyāna; it explains calling the name as 'practice in accord with reality', the three kinds of non-faith, the 'birth of non-birth', the two dharma-bodies, the ten recitations that outweigh a lifetime's evil, the two aspects of merit-transfer (going and returning), and ends by showing from three vows that everything rests on the Buddha's other-power.
notes: T40 is not in the local corpus; all teachings from this text are recalled (no original quoted).

title: Outline of the Meaning of the Pure Land of Peace and Bliss

attribution.tradition: by Tanluan (so headed in the Taishō)

summary: Nine questions and answers on Sukhāvatī: it is not included in the three realms, its adornments, the three grades of aspirants, those born in the 'borderland' or 'womb' because they doubted the Buddha's inconceivable wisdom, how ten continuous recitations can outweigh a lifetime's evil (the Buddha's inconceivable wisdom: a bean of fire burns a hundred years' firewood; a lame man carried by a ship).

title: Verses in Praise of Amitābha Buddha
summary: Tanluan's hymn of homage in seven-character verses, each followed by 'may I with all beings be born in the Land of Peace and Bliss': Amitābha's attainment ten kalpas ago, his twelve names of light, the land and its assembly, and homage to Nāgārjuna; the model of Shinran's Jōdo wasan.

title: Collection on the Land of Peace and Bliss (Anle ji)

structure.description: 2 fascicles, twelve 'great gates' (dàmén), each with sub-sections of scripture citations and questions and answers

summary: Daochuo's anthology urging birth in Sukhāvatī: teaching must fit the time and the capacities of beings; we live in the fourth five-hundred-year period after the Buddha, the age of repentance and calling the name; of the two excellent dharmas, the holy path is hard to realise in the last age and only the Pure Land gate is passable; Amitābha is a reward-body buddha in a reward land; the nianfo samādhi is king of samādhis; ten continuous recitations outweigh a lifetime's evil; the 'intention for another time' objection is refuted; Sukhāvatī is compared with Maitreya's Tuṣita.

title: Commentary on the Contemplation Sūtra (Guanjing shu)
alt_titles: Guanjing sitiemshu 觀經四帖疏 / Kangyō shijōsho
fascicles: Xuanyi fen 玄義分, Xufen yi 序分義, Dingshan yi 定善義, Sanshan yi 散善義

structure.description: 4 fascicles: the essential meaning; the introduction; the meditative good (contemplations 1–13); the non-meditative good (14–16)

summary: Shandao's commentary, written to 'settle the old and the new' interpretations: the Contemplation Sūtra was taught for ordinary beings, all nine grades are ordinary people; Sukhāvatī is a reward land into which ordinary beings are born by the Buddha's vow; the first thirteen contemplations are meditative good, the last three non-meditative good; the three minds (sincere, deep, transferring) with the two kinds of deep entrusting; the five right practices, of which the calling of the name is the rightly determined act 'because it accords with the Buddha's vow'; the parable of the two rivers and the white path; the sūtra's final entrustment of the name shows that the Buddha's intent is exclusive calling of Amitābha's name. Hōnen converted on reading it (1175).
notes: T37 not in the local corpus; teachings from it are recalled, no original quoted.

title: Hymns of Worship for Birth (Wangsheng lizan ji)
alt_titles: Rokuji raisan 六時禮讚 (the six-period hymns)
summary: Shandao's liturgy for worship at the six periods of day and night (sunset, first night, midnight, late night, dawn, noon) using hymns of the Larger Sūtra, Vasubandhu, Yancong, Longshu (Nāgārjuna) and his own; its preface sets out the settled mind, the undertaking and the manner of practice: the three minds, the five gates, the four modes of practice; why calling the name rather than contemplation; 'ten of ten are born' by exclusive practice while mixed practice rarely succeeds.

title: The Dharma Gate of the Merits of the Samādhi of Contemplating the Ocean-like Marks of Amitābha
title_original: 觀念阿彌陀佛相海三昧功德法門
summary: Shandao's manual of the samādhi of contemplating Amitābha (Contemplation Sūtra) and of recollecting him (Pratyutpanna), the procedure for entering a practice hall for one to seven days, confession and vows, instructions for tending the dying, and the 'five kinds of augmenting conditions' by which reciters gain extinction of sins, protection and long life, the vision of the Buddha, embrace, and assurance of birth.

title: Hymns for the Rite of Circumambulation and Sūtra-chanting for Birth (Fashi zan)
title_original: 轉經行道願往生淨土法事讚
summary: Shandao's liturgy (2 fascicles) for chanting the Smaller Sūtra while circumambulating, with hymns of praise and aspiration.

title: Hymns on the Pratyutpanna Practice for Birth, based on the Contemplation Sūtra
title_original: 依觀經等明般舟三昧行道往生讚
summary: Shandao's hymns for the walking pratyutpanna practice, retelling the Contemplation Sūtra's story and exhorting practitioners to birth.

title: Resolving the Many Doubts about the Pure Land (Shi jingtu qunyi lun)
summary: Huaigan's seven fascicles answering objections to Pure Land teaching: the Mahāyānasaṃgraha's 'intention for another time' does not apply to calling the name with sincere practice; the land of sloth and pride (xieman guo) is for those whose practice is mixed; loud recitation readily brings samādhi ('great recitation sees a great buddha, small recitation a small buddha').

title: Ten Doubts about the Pure Land (Jingtu shiyi lun)

attribution.tradition: spoken by the Tiantai master Zhiyi
attribution.scholarly: generally held to be a later (Tang) work attributed to Zhiyi

summary: Ten doubts answered: why bodhisattvas of great compassion should seek birth (a beginner, like a child, cannot yet leave its mother); how seeking birth accords with non-arising (the wise ardently seek birth while understanding that birth has no own-being); why Amitābha rather than any buddha; why the West rather than Tuṣita; how ordinary bound beings are non-retrogressive there (five reasons); how ten recitations suffice; women and the disabled; and the two practices of loathing (impurity contemplation) and joyful aspiration.

title: Five Expedient Gates of Recollecting the Buddha
summary: A short work classifying recollection of the Buddha into five expedient gates, from recollection that brings about the fruit to recollection of the mind-nature (contents recalled only in outline).
notes: Title and attribution from the local CBETA header; contents not read (low confidence on summary).

title: Treatise on the Pure Land (Jiacai)
summary: Jiacai's three-fascicle systematisation of Daochuo's teaching: the bodies and lands of the Buddha, the persons born, the practices, scriptural proofs and records of those born.

title: Essential Resolution on the West, Explaining Doubts (Xifang yaojue)

attribution.tradition: by Kuiji of Da Ci'en si

summary: A Faxiang-attributed defence of birth in the West, answering doubts and comparing Sukhāvatī with Tuṣita; it urges exclusive recollection of Amitābha and dedication of all good roots.

title: Mirror of Recollecting the Buddha (Nianfo jing)

attribution.tradition: compiled by Daojing and Shandao (善道)
attribution.scholarly: the co-compiler Shandao 善道 is usually distinguished from Shandao 善導 (613–681); 8th c.

summary: A Tang anthology arguing the superiority of recollecting the Buddha over other practices, in sections comparing it with them.
notes: Header read locally; content summary low confidence.

title: Treatise on the Jewel-King Samādhi of Recollecting the Buddha
summary: Feixi's three-fascicle treatise in twenty gates presenting recollection of the Buddha — including the recollection of future buddhas in all beings — as the king of samādhis and a direct path.

title: Abbreviated Liturgy of the Five-Tone Recitation (Wuhui nianfo)
title_original: 淨土五會念佛略法事儀讚
summary: Fazhao's liturgy: the nianfo samādhi is 'the truly supreme and profound gate of meditation'; the name is chanted in five 'assemblies' from slow level tone to quick four-syllable recitation, followed by hymns; groups of three to seven chant together with dignity and without seeking fame.

title: Path of the Mind Roaming in Peace and Bliss (Yusim allakdo)

attribution.scholarly: attribution disputed; parts depend on later sources

summary: A Pure Land treatise in seven gates (the teaching's aim, the location of the land, doubts and difficulties, causes of birth, grades of birth, ease and difficulty, resolving doubts), opening with the mind-nature of beings as interpenetrating without obstruction.

title: Doctrinal Essentials of the Sūtra of Immeasurable Life
summary: Wonhyo's outline of the Larger Sūtra: the pure land as the fruit, its causes, the persons born and the doctrine of the four doubts (not read locally).
notes: T37 not local; content summary from memory (moderate).

title: Two Gates of Resolving Doubts and of Practice and Vow for Birth in the Pure Land
title_original: 往生淨土決疑行願二門
summary: Zunshi's two gates: resolving doubts (mind, Buddha and beings are not different, so the land is born in one's own mind; ordinary beings may enter the rightly established group) and practice-and-vow in four parts — worship and repentance, the ten recitations each morning, keeping the Buddha in mind amid affairs, and many kinds of merit.

title: Rite of Repentance and Vows for Birth in the Pure Land
summary: Zunshi's Tiantai-style repentance liturgy in ten sections for practitioners aspiring to Sukhāvatī.

title: Classified Writings on the Land of Bliss (Lebang wenlei)
summary: Zongxiao's five-fascicle anthology of scriptures, treatises, prefaces, biographies and poems on Pure Land; it names Huiyuan the first patriarch of the Lotus society and five successors — Shandao, Fazhao, Shaokang, Shengchang and Zongze.

title: Longshu's Expanded Pure Land Writings
summary: The lay scholar Wang Rixiu's popular exhortation to recite Amitābha's name: faith is the source of the path; instructions for people of every occupation and station; stories of those born.

title: Questions on the Pure Land (Jingtu huowen)
summary: The Yuan Chan master Tianru Weize answers a Chan objector: every land and every mote is the Bliss of mind-only and every buddha is Amitābha of one's own nature, yet to purify the mind there is no method apart from Pure Land practice — contemplation, recollection and the many practices.

title: Precious Mirror of the Lotus School of Lushan
summary: Pudu's ten-fascicle compendium defending the Lotus school against heterodox 'White Lotus' groups: doctrine, practice and biographies from Huiyuan to Mao Ziyuan, whom it presents as the Song reviver of the Lotus society.

title: Direct Pointers to the Jewel-King Samādhi of Recollecting the Buddha
summary: The Ming monk Miaoye's manual presenting recollection of the Buddha as the 'jewel-king' of samādhis, with instructions for practice.

title: Treatise on Birth and Non-birth in the Pure Land
summary: Chuandeng's ten gates in Tiantai terms (one true dharma-realm, the arising of body and land, mind and land identical, beings and buddhas not two, ...) showing that birth in the Pure Land is the birth of non-birth.

title: Comprehensive Treatise on the West (Xifang helun)
summary: The literatus Yuan Hongdao's ten-chapter synthesis of Pure Land with Huayan and Chan.

title: Resolving Doubts about the Pure Land (Jingtu yibian)
summary: Zhuhong's short reply to a Chan objector who calls the Pure Land a mere symbol: 'returning to the source the nature is not two; expedient means have many gates'; Chan and Pure Land reach the same end (quoting Zhongfeng: 'Chan is the Chan of Pure Land; Pure Land is the Pure Land of Chan'); if you truly saw all places as the Pure Land you would live in a latrine without distaste; those who are not sure of ending birth and death should not discard the Pure Land.

title: Commentary and Subcommentary on the Amitābha Sūtra (Amituo jing shuchao)
summary: Zhuhong's major commentary reading the Smaller Sūtra through Huayan: 'holding the name' is of two kinds, holding in phenomena (continuous recitation with faith) and holding in principle (realizing the mind that recites), both leading to the undistracted single mind.
notes: Xuzangjing text not in local corpus; recalled.

title: Collection of Those Born (Wangsheng ji)
summary: Zhuhong's collection of biographies of monks, nuns, rulers, lay men and women and even animals born in the Pure Land, with his comments.

title: Biographies of Those Born in the Pure Land (Jiezhu)
summary: Song collection of biographies of monks born in the Pure Land, from Huiyuan onward.

title: Record of Auspicious Responses of Birth in the Western Pure Land
summary: A Tang collection of short biographies recording the signs — light, fragrance, music, visions of the Buddha — at the deaths of those born in the West.

title: Essential Explanation of the Amitābha Sūtra (Amituo jing yaojie)
summary: Ouyi's commentary in Tiantai terms: the sūtra's essence is the real mark; faith, vow and practice (holding the name) are the three provisions; whether one is born depends entirely on faith and vow, the grade of birth on the depth of holding the name.

title: Ten Essentials of the Pure Land (Jingtu shiyao)
summary: Ouyi's anthology of ten essential Pure Land works (beginning with his own Amitābha Sūtra commentary), later edited by Chengshi.

title: Chapters on the Great Meaning of the Mahāyāna (Huiyuan–Kumārajīva correspondence)
summary: Huiyuan's questions to Kumārajīva and the replies, including the question whether the buddha seen in the pratyutpanna samādhi is a real buddha coming from outside or produced by one's own mind.

title: Comprehensive Record of the Buddhas and Patriarchs (Fozu tongji)
summary: Zhipan's Tiantai history of Buddhism in 54 fascicles; fascicles 26–28 ('Treatise on the Establishment of the Pure Land Teaching') give the seven patriarchs of the Lotus society, the eighteen worthies, and biographies of those born in the Pure Land of every class.

title: Biographies of Eminent Monks (Gaoseng zhuan)
summary: Huijiao's biographies of monks up to 519; the biography of Huiyuan records the vow of 123 persons before an image of Amitābha on Lushan in 402, with Liu Yimin's text of the vow.

title: Commentary on the Meaning of the Contemplation Sūtra (Jingying Huiyuan)
summary: The Sui scholar Jingying Huiyuan's commentary, which ranks the nine grades as sages and ordinary beings of different attainments and treats Sukhāvatī in terms of the three bodies and lands — a reading Shandao set out to correct.

title: Collected Letters and Essays of Master Yinguang
summary: Letters and essays of the 13th Pure Land patriarch urging faith, vow and recitation within ordinary Confucian duties, strict observance of cause and effect, and careful care of the dying.

title: Essentials of Birth (Ōjōyōshū)

structure.description: 3 fascicles, ten great chapters: loathing the defiled realm; seeking the Pure Land; proofs of Sukhāvatī; the right practice of nenbutsu; aids to nenbutsu; nenbutsu at special times (including deathbed practice); benefits; scriptural proofs; other practices for birth; questions

summary: Genshin's anthology of scripture on birth in Sukhāvatī, beginning with vivid accounts of the hells and the six paths to be loathed and the ten pleasures of the Pure Land to be sought; its core is contemplative and oral nenbutsu arranged by Vasubandhu's five gates, with the famous rules for the dying; sent to China and deeply influential in Japan.
notes: Text not in the local corpus; chapter structure and teachings recalled.

title: Records of Japanese Born in the Land of Bliss
summary: The first Japanese collection of lives of those born in the Pure Land (including Prince Shōtoku, Gyōki and Kūya), the model for later ōjōden.

title: Ten Causes of Birth (Ōjō jūin)
summary: Yōkan's ten reasons why one-pointed recitation of Amida's name assures birth.

title: Passages on the Selection of the Nenbutsu in the Original Vow (Senchakushū)

scholarly.text: 1198 CE (Kenkyū 9), at the request of Kujō Kanezane

structure.description: 16 chapters, each a heading, scriptural passages and Hōnen's comment; closes with the 'passage on the threefold selection' and a request to keep the work hidden

summary: Hōnen's argument for the exclusive nenbutsu: following Daochuo, set aside the holy path; following Shandao, set aside miscellaneous practices; the eighteenth vow selected the nenbutsu as the one practice for birth because the name holds all virtues and is easy for all; the three grades, the three minds, the four modes, the Buddha's light embracing reciters, the entrustment of the name to Ānanda and the testimony of all buddhas show the same; 'I rely solely on Shandao'.
notes: Not in local corpus; chapter contents recalled (high for structure).

title: The One-Sheet Document (Ichimai kishōmon)

tradition.text: written two days before Hōnen's death, for Genchi

summary: Hōnen's final summary: the nenbutsu is neither contemplation as taught by scholars of China and Japan nor recitation grounded in understanding its meaning; it is simply to say 'Namu Amida Butsu' in the conviction of being born; the three minds and four modes are contained in that conviction; even those who have learned all the Buddha's teaching should become like the ignorant who know not a letter and just say the nenbutsu.

title: Seven-Article Pledge (Shichikajō kishōmon)

scholarly.text: 1204 CE (Genkyū 1, 11th month), signed by Hōnen and some 190 disciples

summary: Hōnen's pledge, signed by his disciples, forbidding them to attack the doctrines of other schools or other buddhas and bodhisattvas, to dispute with learned men, to say that nenbutsu people need not keep the precepts and may freely do evil, to teach their own ideas as the master's, and similar conduct.
notes: Article order and exact number of signatories recalled (moderate).

title: Record of Attainment of Samādhi (Sanmai hottokki)

attribution.tradition: Hōnen's private record of his samādhi visions (1198–1206), transmitted by Seikan-bō

summary: A record of visions attained in nenbutsu samādhi — the ground, the jewel trees, the ponds and the Buddha's form of the Pure Land — which Hōnen is said to have kept private.

title: Record of the Lamp of the Words of the Saint of Kurodani
alt_titles: Wago tōroku 和語灯録 (Japanese part)
Kango tōroku 漢語灯録 (Chinese part)
summary: Collected letters, sermons and sayings of Hōnen compiled by Ryōe Dōkō, including his letters on one-calling and many-calling and on how to live so as to say the nenbutsu.

title: Illustrated Biography of Hōnen in 48 Scrolls
summary: The standard Jōdo-shū biography of Hōnen: his father's dying injunction not to seek revenge, his Tendai training, his conversion on reading Shandao (1175), the Ōhara dialogue, the Senchakushū, the persecution and exile, his death reciting the nenbutsu.

title: Nenbutsu Seal of Transmission for the Last Age
summary: Benchō's work setting out the transmission of Hōnen's teaching (the settled mind, practice and manner of practice) as received by his line.
notes: Date and content outline low confidence.

title: Distinguishing One-Calling and Many-Calling
summary: Ryūkan's short tract warning against both extremes in the dispute on one-calling and many-calling; Shinran annotated its scriptural passages in his Ichinen tanen mon'i.

title: On Faith Alone (Yuishinshō)
summary: Seikaku's exposition of Hōnen's teaching: the holy path and the Pure Land path, the nenbutsu of the primal vow among the Pure Land practices, the three minds, and the single calling; recommended repeatedly by Shinran to his followers.

title: The True Teaching, Practice and Realization of the Pure Land Way (Kyōgyōshinshō)
title_original: 顕浄土真実教行証文類

tradition.text: 1224 (Gennin 1), the year Honganji takes as the founding of Shinshū

scholarly.text: drafted in the Kantō from the 1220s and revised until the 1250s (Bandō autograph)

structure.description: general preface; six chapters: Teaching (kyō), Practice (gyō, ending with the Shōshinge), Shinjin (with its own preface), Realization (shō), True Buddha and Land, Transformed Buddhas and Lands (with the postscript on the persecution of 1207); 6 fascicles

summary: Shinran's systematic anthology: the true teaching is the Larger Sūtra, whose purport is the primal vow and whose substance is the name; the great practice is saying the name of the Tathāgata of Unhindered Light; great shinjin, the entrusting given by Amida, is the true cause; realization is necessary attainment of nirvāṇa (eleventh vow) and the return to save beings; the true Buddha and land are of immeasurable light and life; other practices and self-power nenbutsu are provisional gates leading to transformed lands; non-Buddhist paths and deities are not to be relied on.
notes: Not in local corpus; recalled at chapter level.

title: Hymn of True Entrusting and the Nenbutsu (Shōshin nenbutsu ge)
summary: The hymn recited daily in Shinshū: homage to Amida; the vow and the name as the rightly determined act and shinjin as the cause; the evil and good ordinary beings who hear and entrust being called white lotuses; then the teachings of the seven masters from Nāgārjuna to Hōnen.

title: Hymns of the Pure Land (Jōdo wasan)
summary: 118 Japanese hymns on Amida, the three sūtras and the Pure Land, including hymns on the benefits in this life and on shinjin as buddha-nature.
notes: The three are together called the Sanjō wasan.

title: Hymns of the Pure Land Masters (Kōsō wasan)
summary: 117 hymns praising the seven masters: Nāgārjuna, Vasubandhu, Tanluan, Daochuo, Shandao, Genshin and Hōnen.
notes: The three are together called the Sanjō wasan.

title: Hymns of the Dharma Ages (Shōzōmatsu wasan)
summary: Hymns composed in old age on the three ages of the Dharma, doubt of the Buddha's wisdom, and Shinran's lament over his own untruthful heart; with the appended note on jinen hōni in some versions.
notes: The three are together called the Sanjō wasan.

title: Notes on 'Essentials of Faith Alone' (Yuishinshō mon'i)
summary: Shinran's glosses, in plain Japanese for 'people of the countryside who do not know the meaning of characters', on the scriptural passages quoted in Seikaku's Yuishinshō: the name, entrusting, the Buddha's light, the dharma-body as suchness that fills the world.

title: Notes on Once-calling and Many-calling (Ichinen tanen mon'i)
summary: Shinran's glosses on passages concerning one and many callings, concluding that one should not insist on either; explains 'immediately attain birth and dwell in non-retrogression' as attainment in this life at the moment of shinjin.

title: Lamp for the Latter Ages (Mattōshō)
summary: Twenty-two letters of Shinran: the welcoming at death belongs to birth by various practices, while the person of shinjin is already among the truly settled; do not take poison because there is an antidote; the letter on jinen hōni; the person of shinjin is equal to the Tathāgatas.
notes: Letter numbering varies between editions; numbers given are those commonly used (moderate).

title: Gutoku's Notes (Gutokushō)
summary: Shinran's classification of the Buddhist teachings into two pairs and four levels — vertical and crosswise, going out and transcending — with the Pure Land path of the primal vow as crosswise transcendence.

title: A Record in Lament of Divergences (Tannishō)

attribution.tradition: words of Shinran recorded by his disciple (identified with Yuien of Kawada)
attribution.scholarly: Yuien's authorship is the prevailing view

structure.description: preface; ten sections of Shinran's words; eight sections lamenting divergent views; postscript; Rennyo's colophon restricting it

summary: Sayings of Shinran and the compiler's laments: the moment one entrusts oneself to the inconceivable vow and the thought of saying the nenbutsu arises, one is embraced never to be abandoned; even a good person attains birth, how much more an evil person; Shinran has not one disciple; the nenbutsu is the single path free of hindrance, neither practice nor good; 'in the nenbutsu, no working is true working'; the vow was 'for me, Shinran, alone'; only the nenbutsu is true.
notes: Section numbering standard; wording recalled, no original quoted.

title: Letters of Eshinni
summary: Letters of Shinran's wife to their daughter Kakushinni recounting Shinran's hundred-day retreat at the Rokkakudō, his going to Hōnen, her dream that Hōnen was Seishi (Mahāsthāmaprāpta) and Shinran Kannon, and his abandoned attempt to read the three sūtras a thousand times for the people's benefit.

title: Biography of Shinran (Godenshō / Honganji Shōnin Shinran den'e)
summary: Kakunyo's illustrated biography of Shinran used liturgically in Honganji at Hōonkō: the Rokkakudō dream verse, the debates in Hōnen's circle on shinjin, the exile and death.

title: Record of the Oral Transmission (Kudenshō)
summary: Kakunyo's record of sayings of Shinran said to have been transmitted through Nyoshin, used to assert Honganji's lineage.

title: Correcting Heresy (Gaijashō)
summary: Kakunyo's list of deviations in Shinshū communities (such as naming lineage registers and conduct of rival groups) to be corrected.

title: The Letters of Rennyo (Ofumi / Gobunshō)

scholarly.text: 1461–1498; five fascicles of 80 letters selected in the early 16th c.

summary: Rennyo's letters in plain Japanese: abandon miscellaneous practices and single-heartedly rely on Amida to save you in the one great matter of the afterlife; then the nenbutsu is said in gratitude; the person and the Dharma are one in Namu Amida Butsu; follow the laws of the land and do not disparage other buddhas and kami; the letter on white ashes.

title: Record of Things Heard from Rennyo
title_original: 蓮如上人御一代記聞書
summary: Sayings of Rennyo recorded by those close to him, on shinjin, gratitude and the conduct of followers.

title: On the Settled Mind (Anjin ketsujōshō)

attribution.scholarly: probably from a Seizan milieu, 14th c.

summary: A tract teaching that the Buddha's attainment of awakening and the beings' birth were accomplished together, so that the person and the Dharma are one (kihō ittai) in Namu Amida Butsu.

title: Illustrated Biography of the Holy Man Ippen (Ippen Hijiri-e)
summary: Twelve scrolls of Ippen's life and teaching: study under Shōtatsu, the refusal of the talisman by a monk and the Kumano oracle of 1274, the distribution of talismans, the first dancing nenbutsu (1279), his wanderings, burning of his books and death (1289).
notes: Scroll numbers for episodes are approximate (low).

title: Recorded Sayings of Ippen (Ippen shōnin goroku)

attribution.scholarly: compiled 1763 by the Ji-shū; relies on earlier collections

summary: Hymns, letters and sayings of Ippen: casting off everything, the name alone, the practitioner's mind not to be relied on.

title: Illustrated Origins of the Interfusing Nenbutsu (Yūzū nenbutsu engi)
summary: Scrolls telling of Amida's revelation to Ryōnin and of the enrolment of gods and people in the nenbutsu register.

title: Wheel Crushing Heresy (Zaijarin)
summary: Myōe's refutation of the Senchakushū, charging above all that Hōnen discards the aspiration for awakening (bodhicitta), which the sūtras make the cause of birth, and that he likens the practitioners of the holy path to bandits (in the two-rivers parable).

title: Petition of Kōfukuji (Kōfukuji sōjō)
summary: Petition to the court drafted by Jōkei asking for the suppression of the exclusive nenbutsu, listing nine errors: establishing a new school without authorization, a new image, slighting Śākyamuni, hindering the good practices, turning against the kami, ignorance of the Pure Land, misunderstanding the nenbutsu, harming the Buddhist community, and disturbing the nation.

title: Lamp for the Last Age of the Dharma (Mappō tōmyōki)

attribution.scholarly: generally regarded as a later work (late Heian)

summary: Argues that in the last age there are only monks in name, without precepts; they should nevertheless be honoured as treasures; much quoted by Shinran in the Kyōgyōshinshō.

title: Fragrant Sayings (Ichigon hōdan)
summary: Short sayings of Pure Land hijiri and Hōnen's circle on renunciation, the transience of life and reliance on the nenbutsu.
